title: The Tea Master in the Snow
teaser: A Japanese lord with no prospects spent his youth on tea. His phrase for treating every gathering as the only one outlived him.
story: Ii Naosuke was born the fourteenth son of Ii Naonaka, lord of the castle domain of Hikone in central Japan. With so many brothers ahead of him, no one expected him to rule. In 1831, at 17, he moved into a small house in the castle grounds and named it Umoregi-no-ya, the Bogwood House, after wood that lies buried in mud. In a short essay of 1835 he wrote that, even as a piece of buried wood, he would 'continue to cultivate those arts required by my station'.

Those arts included poetry, painting, calligraphy, the martial arts and, above all, tea. He became a master of the Sekishū school of chanoyu, the formal preparing and serving of tea, and wrote about it for most of his life. Then his brothers died or were adopted into other families, and in 1850 the buried wood became lord of Hikone.

Around 1857 he finished a short book, Chanoyu ichie shū, which one historian translates as 'Collection for a Tea Gathering'. Its opening borrows a thought from Yamanoue Sōji, a pupil of the great sixteenth-century tea master Sen no Rikyū. Sōji had written that a guest should behave, from entering the garden to leaving, 'as though it were a meeting that could occur only once in the lifetime'. Naosuke pressed that thought into four characters. In H. Paul Varley's translation, a tea gathering is something 'which we can speak of as "one time, one meeting"'. Host and guests may meet often, he explained, but 'one day's gathering can never be repeated exactly'.

That is ichi-go ichi-e. Each meeting is unrepeatable, so the host must take care over every detail, and the guests must give it their full attention in return. Naosuke added a second idea: when the guests have gone, the host should sit alone for a time before the hearth and reflect on the gathering that has just ended.

He had little time left to practise either. In 1858 he was made tairō, the shogunate's chief minister. The last entry in his surviving record of tea gatherings is dated five days after the appointment. That year he had a trade treaty with the United States signed without the emperor's approval, and then punished more than 100 of his opponents in what became known as the Ansei Purge. On the morning of 24 March 1860, after heavy snow, 18 men, 17 of them from the Mito domain, attacked his procession outside the Sakurada Gate of Edo Castle and killed him.

His phrase outlived him. It is brushed on scrolls hung in tea rooms and borrowed far beyond them, as a reminder that the dinner, the conversation or the walk you are in now will not come again in quite this form.
takeaway: Ichi-go ichi-e, 'one time, one meeting': because no gathering can ever be repeated exactly, treat each one as the only one, and give it your full care and attention.

recall.question: As a young man, Wang Yangming sat for seven days in front of some bamboo, trying to find its principle, and fell ill. What idea did he later teach instead?
recall.answer: The unity of knowledge and action: truly knowing what is right already moves you to do it, so knowing without doing isn't really knowing.

rabbitHole.title: Once in a lifetime, every time
rabbitHole.intro: Who really said it, does thinking about endings make us enjoy things more, and what happens when a musician lives by it? Pour another cup.

levels.heading: Not quite Rikyū's words
body: The popular version credits ichi-go ichi-e to Sen no Rikyū himself, as an old Zen saying. The evidence is more layered. The idea goes back to Rikyū's circle: the tea school Omotesenke traces it to an expression of his, 'one chance in a lifetime'. The written source is his pupil Yamanoue Sōji, whose record, in a copy dated 1588 and thought to be in his own hand, told guests to treat a gathering as if it could happen only once.

The four-character phrase itself is Naosuke's. The historian Melinda Landeck, in her 2015 study of warlord tea, notes that the accepted definition is usually attributed to him and that he condensed the second half of Sōji's sentence into it. Sōji did not live to see his idea last. In 1590, after the fall of the Hōjō clan he served, Toyotomi Hideyoshi had him mutilated and executed.

levels.heading: The bittersweet effect
body: Is there anything in the idea that endings sharpen enjoyment? The psychologist Jaime Kurtz tested a version of it on college seniors about six weeks before graduation. For two weeks they wrote about their college lives, with graduation framed either as very close or as far off.

In her 2008 paper in Psychological Science, students for whom the end felt near reported taking part in more college activities. In her doctoral research at the University of Virginia, across three studies, those in the 'close' condition also reported greater well-being and appreciation of college life, and did more things like spending time with friends and taking scenic routes to class. Kurtz was candid that the results were 'not entirely consistent across studies'. Her conclusion, in her own words, was that 'thinking about an experience's future ending can enhance one's present experience of it'. It is a modest, careful finding, not a law of happiness.

levels.heading: The conductor who would not record
body: The Romanian conductor Sergiu Celibidache met the Buddhist monk Martin Steinke in Berlin in 1939, and Zen shaped his outlook for the rest of his life. Accounts of his work link his music-making to ideas such as ichi-go ichi-e, the moment that never recurs.

He drew a practical conclusion. After one recording contract in 1948, he refused to release commercial recordings, arguing that a listener could not have a transcendent experience outside the concert hall and that recordings gave only a distorted picture. He led the Munich Philharmonic from 1979 until his death in 1996. The twist is that he allowed radio broadcasts, so almost all his concerts were taped anyway. After his death, with his family's consent, many were released by EMI and Deutsche Grammophon, letting listeners replay, again and again, performances he had meant to happen once.

furtherReading.note: Scholarly essays on the history of tea, including Varley's translation of Naosuke's 'one time, one meeting'.

furtherReading.title: Aesthetic Authorities: The Socio-Political Dimensions of Warlord Tea Praxis in Early Modern Japan, 1573–1860
furtherReading.author: Melinda Sue Landeck, PhD dissertation, University of Kansas (2015)
furtherReading.note: Chapter Five is a detailed study of Naosuke as a tea master and politician.

furtherReading.author: Jaime L. Kurtz, Psychological Science (2008)
furtherReading.note: The graduation study on how imagining an ending changes how we live the present.

lookingGlass.heading: The quiet tea room was also a political one
body: The gentle picture of ichi-go ichi-e, a Zen-minded host savouring an unrepeatable afternoon, is not the whole story. Varley described Naosuke as much influenced by Zen and his tea as quietist and contemplative. Landeck argues that this Buddhist reading is overstated. Drawing on Tanimura Reiko's study of 44 gatherings Naosuke hosted, she notes that his guests were mostly fellow warriors, and that his gatherings shifted from quiet meetings among friends towards something more political. The tea room became, in effect, a place for political networking.

None of that makes the principle false. It does show that the same careful hospitality can serve sincere attention and calculated alliance-building at once, and that a lovely phrase is no guarantee of the motives of the person using it.
lookingGlass.verdict: Where that leaves you: the history of the phrase is solid and the idea is a sound guide to hosting and paying attention, but treat it as a practice to try, not a proven route to happiness, and judge its users by what they do.

quiz.question: Where did Ii Naosuke find the thought he condensed into 'ichi-go ichi-e'?
options: In the writings of Yamanoue Sōji, a pupil of Sen no Rikyū
In the terms of a trade treaty with the United States
In a poem carved over the Sakurada Gate of Edo Castle
In a letter from the emperor
quiz.explain: Sōji wrote that a guest should behave 'as though it were a meeting that could occur only once in the lifetime', and Naosuke pressed that into four characters.

quiz.question: Which of these best captures ichi-go ichi-e?
options: Treat each gathering with full care, because it can never be repeated exactly
Invite the same guests often, so that each meeting goes more smoothly
Keep tea gatherings short, so that no one grows bored
Make tea look effortless, however hard it really is
quiz.explain: Naosuke wrote that host and guests may meet often, but 'one day's gathering can never be repeated exactly', so every detail deserves care.
